source.title: Quiet Feature Learning in Algorithmic Tasks
source.authors: Prudhviraj Naidu; Zixian Wang; Leon Bergen; R. Paturi

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports phase transitions and feature learning in algorithmic tasks, but does not measure induction heads, their formation, or in-context learning as defined in the claim. It cites prior work on phase transitions in in-context learning.
record.gate_note: The paper's own algorithmic-task findings are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version; they do not test an induction-head version. The mention of Olsson et al. is background, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study trains Transformer++ models on synthetic algorithmic tasks and reports loss phase transitions, probed intermediate features and feature ablations. It never measures induction heads, previous-token heads, or in-context learning (loss vs token index). Olsson et al. (2022) appears only in related work on phase transitions. The loss-plateau/quiet-feature findings resemble V2/V7 themes, but they concern a different construct, so they go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that models on algorithmic tasks encode causally necessary intermediate computations (quiet features) well before loss improves. They argue this shows cross-entropy loss is a poor proxy for learning and motivates richer training diagnostics.
record.recipe_differences: No induction-head method is applied. The paper probes and ablates algorithm-specific intermediate features in Transformer++ models trained on synthetic algorithmic tasks.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature emergence varies by task and token position: early positions are learned first for addition, multiplication, and maximum subarray, while later positions are learned first for breadth-first search. Ablation effects also vary by task, input size, and feature.

fits_no_version.finding: In single-epoch training on algorithmic tasks, compute-optimal and within-run validation loss plateaus, then drops abruptly. Probed intermediate features (quiet features) emerge during the plateau.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abrupt loss transitions on algorithmic tasks are preceded by hidden internal feature learning, so loss curves understate representational progress.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating probed quiet-feature directions lowers test accuracy more than random-direction ablation for most features. First operand at size 16 shows no effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-transition algorithmic features are often causally necessary for final task performance, depending on the feature and input size.

record.problems: The reported findings concern synthetic algorithmic tasks rather than induction heads or natural-language in-context learning. The phase-transition trajectories are primarily presented in figures; exact loss values for the aggregate transition are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Other task-specific scaling-law plots and feature-ablation loss values in Technical Appendix Table 6 are not separately recorded because they do not add a distinct induction-head or in-context-learning result.

untested.parts: Abrupt induction-head formation coinciding with in-context-learning gain and loss bump
Induction heads as the mechanism of most in-context learning in large models
Induction heads across families, sizes, runs, architectures
Data/training dependence of induction-head formation or in-context-learning persistence
Other mechanisms carrying few-shot task learning
Multi-step or overlapping transitions in induction-head formation

record.verdict_notes: No induction-head or in-context-learning measurement anywhere in the text. The record's relation, tranche and none-links are correct. Some row states (e.g., partial/absent on ablations) describe ablation effect size, not a claim version; they are harmless.

versions.untested_parts: Induction-head formation, previous-token-head composition, and the [A][B] … [A] → [B] behavior.
Whether induction heads form abruptly, or whether their formation coincides with an in-context-learning gain and a loss bump.
Induction heads' contribution to most in-context learning in large transformers.
Induction behavior across model families, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.
Dependence of induction-head formation or in-context learning on data or training setup.
Whether other mechanisms carry few-shot task learning instead of induction heads.
Whether induction-head formation comprises multiple sub-steps or overlapping transitions.
